sm: Host Kato Del and Wall Street Journal editorial board colleague Elliot Kaufman discuss Vice President J.D. Vance's social media post saying Republicans lost this week because of the war in Iran. Kaufman says the war and the gasoline prices tied to it were one reason, but not the only one. He points to exit polls where voters ranked corruption first and cost of living second, and notes Trump's approval on prices was already at Biden levels before the war, partly because of tariffs. He adds that voters dislike tariffs and immigration enforcement overreach by similar margins, and that most voters want the same or a more active US role in the world, including 75 percent of Republicans. Kaufman suggests Vance has political reasons to focus on one factor ahead of a possible 2028 run.

Kaufman finds it odd that Vance listed changing the US relationship with Israel among the causes of the defeat. He notes that foreign policy was the top issue for only 4 percent of voters, and that Republican voters remain broadly supportive of Israel. The hosts then play Trump's response, in which he said he knew the war would have an impact but that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, and he later said he would do it again. Kaufman says Trump did not sell the war because he expected a quick one, citing his promises of four weeks and then four to six weeks, the Venezuela operation, and the twelve-day war with Iran. Trump thought he would need no congressional buy-in, no allies and perhaps not even public support, which proved a mistake.

Kaufman argues that once the war dragged on, the administration pulled back instead of escalating. He says a ceasefire that was not really a ceasefire, then a memorandum of understanding promising Iran sanctions relief, let Iran claim ownership of the Strait of Hormuz, so the war looked aimless by the time the blockade began. Del notes the administration's best argument was that Iran was mass-producing conventional missiles as a shield around its nuclear program. Kaufman agrees there was real strategic logic, but says Trump never made that case and that Democrats' line about a war of choice succeeded partly because the administration saw a generational opportunity after Iran was weakened. He adds that airstrikes alone struggle against deeply buried missile sites, and that special forces raids would be needed, with no appetite for that and no public case made. The hosts then turn to Vance's long-known opposition to the war.

The hosts ask whether Vance can credibly stay on as a lead negotiator with Iran after saying publicly that the war was not worth it. Kaufman says Vance is no longer a credible messenger for threats of force, which undermines Trump just as the US position was strengthening, since the Navy has restored traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. He expects Iran to make no concessions, and notes that Congressman Ro Khanna wants a funding bill barring money for military action in Iran. Kaufman describes the administration's options, which include continuing negotiations, keeping the blockade going, or seeking a decisive result. He criticizes the escalate-to-deescalate approach, saying Iran's regime has openly predicted midterm losses would make Trump give in. If the goal is the nuclear program, he says two untouched assets remain, the Pickaxe Mountain enrichment site and the enriched uranium buried under the Esfahan complex.

Kaufman says reaching those two sites would require a risky special forces operation. If the goal is overthrowing the regime, he says the options are a massive military blitz or a long naval blockade that cuts off Iran's trade, and a short burst of strikes is least likely to work. He says Pete Hegseth may become a scapegoat, though he was less involved than expected, and he would not want Admiral Brad Cooper to pay a price. He warns that one faction wants any deal, even handing Iran effective control of the Strait of Hormuz, and voters would see that as a defeat. His lessons are not to start a war without public buy-in and not to wrap it up prematurely, and not to conclude presidents can never win support for sustained sacrifice. He closes by saying the constant will-he-won't-he approach undermined credibility with voters and with Iran, and the question is whether the administration reads the loss narrowly and gives Iran what it wants.
